y5-0: More movement, slower progression in Parkinson’s
y5-2: Nearly a billion people could have osteoarthritis by 2050
y5-3: Could an epilepsy drug protect cartilage? So far, only in the lab
y5-4: In a study published in Neurology on 7 October 2026 by researchers at the University of Cincinnati in the USA, 294 people with mild to moderate Parkinson’s disease were followed for up to 7 years. In those who did more than 8 hours a week of moderate or vigorous physical activity (including work, housework and hobbies), decline in thinking skills and worsening of movement symptoms were slower than in those who did less than 4 hours. A similar link was seen when looking at total time, intensity-weighted amount and vigorous activity alone.
y5-5: This is an observational study: it does not prove that movement slows the disease. Activity was measured by questionnaire, based on what people reported, and the differences between the groups were small; according to the researchers, these small differences may become meaningful over the years. Still, it is one more piece of evidence for how valuable regular movement is in Parkinson’s.
y5-6: Sources: American Academy of Neurology (EurekAlert), 7 October 2026 · U.S. News, 8 October 2026
y5-7: According to a global health policy roadmap published in The Lancet in October 2026 and led by Curtin University in Australia, about 600 million people had osteoarthritis in 2023; this number could approach one billion by 2050. The disability burden caused by osteoarthritis rose by 65% between 1990 and 2023. An ageing population, rising obesity and joint injuries are given as the main drivers of the increase.
y5-8: The authors call for osteoarthritis not to be seen as an inevitable part of ageing, for it to be built into primary care and rehabilitation, and for low-value treatments to be reduced while approaches that support movement become more widely available. In knee osteoarthritis, excess weight and joint injuries are modifiable risk factors. In an Australian study from 2009–10, only 43% of osteoarthritis care encounters met best-practice standards.
y5-9: Sources: Knowridge, 14 October 2026 · Medical Xpress, October 2026
y5-10: In a study at Yale School of Medicine published in Bioactive Materials, lacosamide, a drug used to treat epilepsy, steered cartilage cells away from breakdown and towards repair by blocking a sodium channel called Nav1.7, which is overactive in osteoarthritic joints. The researchers delivered the drug into the joint inside a collagen gel that sets at body temperature and releases it slowly over several weeks; a single injection every four weeks protected the cartilage better than the drug given by mouth every day.
y5-11: The findings come only from cell and animal experiments; the drug has never been tested for osteoarthritis in people. The effective dose range is narrow and its long-term safety is unknown. So it is far too early to use it for osteoarthritis; today, the approaches with the strongest evidence are exercise, weight management and understanding the condition.
y5-12: Sources: ScienceDaily (Yale School of Medicine), 8 October 2026 · Bioactive Materials, 2026
